# FDG9157

> DO position the output buffer parameter (“destination”) as the first method parameter after the source parameter(s).

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 9.12.1 Data Transformation Operations.

## How it is checked

- Check: fdg (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: FDG9157
- Automatic fix: not applied automatically (the fix can break callers)
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test none
- Status: verified

Message: Move the output buffer '{0}' of '{1}' after the source parameter '{2}'

FDG9157 reports a parameter named destination of an output buffer type (Span<T>, Memory<T>, an array or ArraySegment<T>) of an externally visible method when a parameter named source comes after it. Other parameters before destination are not reported: the source can be an input value of any type (the TryWriteGuid call of the FDG9169 example passes a Guid before the destination), which symbols cannot tell from the other parameters. The body's request that an offset immediately follow its array is not checked, nor are outputs with other names (ciphertext, tag), overrides and interface implementations, so coverage is partial. Span<T> and Memory<T> types need .NET Core 2.1 or later, or the System.Memory package on .NET Framework and .NET Standard 2.0 (see FDG9137). Reordering changes the public signature, so the fix is breaking; there is no code fix.

## From the book

Some methods—instance methods, in particular—may provide the source from ambient state; therefore, no formal source parameter is required. When a formal source parameter is required, it should be the first parameter, followed by the destination parameter, and then any other parameters.

```csharp
public partial class IncrementalHash {
  // No source parameter is required,
  // because the values were built by other instance methods.
  public bool TryGetHashAndReset(
    Span<byte> destination,
    out int bytesWritten) { ... }
}

public partial class ByteOperations {
  // One source, one destination
  // (destination is read-write in this example).
  public static int XorInto(
    ReadOnlySpan<byte> source,
    Span<byte> destination) { ... }

  // Two source parameters, one destination.
  // The source parameters come first.
  public static int Xor(
    ReadOnlySpan<byte> left,
    ReadOnlySpan<byte> right,
    Span<byte> destination) { ... }

  // One source, one destination, one other parameter.
  public static int CombineInto(
    ReadOnlySpan<byte> source,
    Span<byte> destination,
    BitOperation operation) { ... }

  // Two sources, one destination, one other parameter.
  public static int Combine(
    ReadOnlySpan<byte> left,
    ReadOnlySpan<byte> right,
    Span<byte> destination,
    BitOperation operation) { ... }
}

public partial class AesGcm {
  // Two (or three) inputs, two outputs.
  public void Encrypt(
    ReadOnlySpan<byte> nonce,
    ReadOnlySpan<byte> plaintext,
    Span<byte> ciphertext,
    Span<byte> tag,
    ReadOnlySpan<byte> associatedData = default) { ... }
}
```

When a buffer-writing method accepts an array and an offset, the offset parameter should immediately follow the array it is associated with. This is one of the only reasons for inserting a parameter between the `source` and `destination` parameters.

```csharp
public static int XorInto(
  ReadOnlySpan<byte> source,
  Span<byte> destination) { ... }

public static int XorInto(
  byte[] source,
  byte[] destination) { ... }

public static int XorInto(
  byte[] source, int sourceIndex,
  byte[] destination, int destinationIndex) { ... }
```
